title: Working into both sides of a foundation chain
subtitle: How to work into the top loops and the back bumps of the same starting chain
excerpt: Working into both sides of a foundation chain means crocheting along the top of the chain for the first row, then turning and working into the exposed lower loops (the back bumps) to create stitches pointing in the opposite direction. This technique is used to start oval shapes, two-directional fabric, and bag bases.
sourceNotes: Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopedia of Needlework, 1886, Project Gutenberg #20776. Edie Eckman, The Crochet Answer Book (Storey Publishing).

glossaryTerms.definition: The horizontal loop on the underside of a foundation chain, running along the bottom edge. Working into the back bump instead of the top two loops leaves the top loops visible and accessible for a second row of stitches.

A flat crochet shape formed by working along one side of a foundation chain and then continuing around the other side. The chain length determines the length of the oval; the number of stitches at each end determines its width.

content.text: Working into both sides of a foundation chain produces an

. The first pass works into the top two loops of the chain from one end to the other; at the far end, instead of turning and going back, the work continues around the end and comes back down the other side, working into the
of the same chain. The result is an oval: two straight sides joined by rounded ends. This is the standard starting method for oval bag bases, amigurumi feet, and tote bag floors.

items.name: Yarn and hook appropriate to the project
Stitch markers
items.note: Two: one for the beginning of the round, one for the centre back where the two ends of the chain meet after rounding.

content.text: Make the foundation chain to the length specified by the pattern. The number of stitches in the oval base will be approximately twice the number of chains minus the end stitches.
Insert a stitch marker in the first chain. This marks the beginning of the round when the oval is closed at the end.

Work your first row of stitches into the top two loops of each chain, starting from the second chain from the hook and working toward the far end of the chain. At the last chain, work the number of stitches the pattern specifies for the end (commonly 3 or 4 double crochet into the same chain) to round the end.
Without turning the work, continue back along the underside of the chain. Work into the

of each chain from the far end back to the near end. These bumps sit on the underside of the chain and are slightly harder to see than the top loops. Use the hook tip to feel for each bump if the yarn is dark.
At the near end (the first chain), work the same number of rounding stitches as you worked at the far end. Slip stitch into the first stitch of the round (or the marked stitch) to close the oval.
Subsequent rounds work into each stitch around the oval and increase at the short ends to keep the fabric flat, as in working a flat circle in the round.

items.symptom: The oval base is puckering at the short ends
items.cause: Too few increase stitches at the end of the chain. The straight-side stitches curve around the end without adding enough width.
items.fix: On the next round, work additional increases at each end. For a flat oval, each short end needs roughly as many extra stitches as the straight side has in total rows.

items.symptom: The back bump row of stitches is visibly looser than the top-loop row
items.cause: The back bump sits in a slightly different plane from the top loops and may pull more yarn than expected.
items.fix: Work the back bump row one hook size smaller if the looseness is significant. Alternatively, tension the yarn more firmly on the return side.

items.symptom: The oval is twisting instead of lying flat
items.cause: The work rotated between the first and second sides of the chain, reversing the orientation.
items.fix: The oval base should be worked without turning at the far end: the hook simply continues in the same direction, curves around the last chain, and comes back. Check that the work was not flipped over at the turning point.

content.text: Work a simple tote bag base: chain 30, work double crochet into both sides for a 10 cm by 20 cm oval. This produces a solid fabric floor that is stronger than working from a magic ring because the load is distributed along the length of the chain rather than pulling on a single central knot.
